records.content: Human exposure to rabies is on the rise this summer, warns the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . According to a CDC health advisory issued Sept. 10, "multiple United States jurisdictions" have reported increases in human exposure to rabies or animals in which rabies is less commonly reported since July 2026. The advisory notes "high-profile rabies outbreaks and mass rabies exposure events." Those outbreaks include one in North Carolina, where baby goats at a mobile petting zoo were infected with rabies. Visitors may have been exposed to rabies at 10 locations between July 28 and Aug. 27. The CDC received 17% more rabies-related inquiries from July to August 2026 than during the same period in 2025, including reports of mass exposure events involving more than one person. According to weekly pharmacy data as of Sept. 2, 2026, utilization for the two rabies vaccines and the two rabies immunoglobulins licensed in the United States increased by an estimated 33% and 76%, respectively, compared with the same time period last year. Here's how to protect yourself from rabies. On Aug. 19, a raccoon tested positive for rabies in the area of Steele Drive in Tyaskin. 'Forbidden ravioli': Raccoon rabies baiting in Ohio. Is your dog safe? What is rabies? Rabies is a fatal but preventable viral disease, according to its CDC entry . It primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to severe brain disease and death if medical care is not received before symptoms start. How is rabies spread? It can be spread to people and pets through the bites and scratches of an infected animal. What are the symptoms of rabies? It can take weeks or months from the time of exposure for symptoms of rabies to show. And once clinical signs appear, the disease is almost always fatal. The first symptoms of rabies may include: Flu-like illness including weakness or discomfort, fever, or headache Discomfort, prickling or an itching sensation at the site of the bite Symptoms of advanced rabies include: Being very thirsty but panicked by fluids Aggressive behavior like thrashing and biting Experts say any potential human or pet contact with a bat should be reported and evaluated to rule out rabies exposure. What animals carry rabies? Do mosquitoes carry rabies? More than 90% of reported cases of rabies in animals occur in wildlife. Rabies is found in many wildlife species, including: Just askin': So, you trapped a live raccoon on your property in Ohio. Now what? Rabies in dogs Rabid dogs in the Unites States are uncommon because of effective vaccination and control programs, the CDC states. Worldwide, however, domestic dogs are responsible for the roughly 70,000 human deaths from rabies each year. Who is at risk for rabies? People most at risk for rabies include: Travelers, especially in areas where rabid dogs are still a problem Outdoor enthusiasts who may come into contact with rabid wildlife Veterinary professionals, animal control workers, wildlife researchers or rehabilitators, agricultural workers or others who work in contact with animals. People who are at increased risk for rabies exposures may want to consider pre-exposure vaccination for increased protection. How can you prevent rabies? The CDC says human cases of rabies in the United States are rare, thanks to prevention efforts of veterinarians who vaccinate more than 90 million dogs and cats each year, wildlife management officials and public health professionals. More than 5 million vaccine baits are distributed yearly to wildlife to control rabies in animals. You can help prevent rabies by: Making sure your pets are up to date on their rabies vaccines. Keeping wildlife wild — stay away from wildlife for both human and animal safety. Calling animal control to remove stray animals from your neighborhood. Washing bites or scratches immediately with soap and water after possible rabies exposure. Seeking medical care urgently if you may have been exposed to rabies. records.content: Connecticut has not had a human rabies case since the 1990s, state health officials said, but the virus continues to turn up in animals each year as federal officials warn doctors and health departments about an increase in rabies exposures and treatment errors nationwide. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention issued a health advisory this week after reporting a 17% increase in rabies-related inquiries from July through August compared with the same period last year. The CDC also said at least eight state health departments reported increased use of post-exposure rabies treatment, treatment errors or both, but did not release which ones. The advisory is not a warning that human rabies is common. Human rabies remains rare in the United States, but the disease is almost always fatal once symptoms begin, making fast assessment and proper treatment critical after possible exposure. In Connecticut , rabies remains primarily an animal-health and exposure-response issue. The Connecticut Public Health Laboratory tested 1,022 animals for rabies in fiscal year 2025, and 40 tested positive, according to the state Department of Public Health's 2025 Administrative Digest . The lab is the only laboratory in the state authorized to test animals involved in human exposures. The state's modern rabies history began in 1991 , when raccoon rabies was first found in Fairfield County after spreading from New York. The virus reached all eight Connecticut counties over the next several years and has remained present in the state's wildlife population since then. DPH's most recent annual rabies report available online , from 2023, listed 36 confirmed rabid animals statewide, including bats, raccoons, skunks, cats, groundhogs, a bobcat and a fox. The state's rabies data, however, are not a complete census of rabies in the wild. Animals are generally tested when a person or domestic animal may have been exposed, meaning the numbers reflect both animal infections and human encounters. DEEP said it works closely with DPH and the state Department of Agriculture to monitor rabies as part of the state's One Health efforts, a public-health approach that recognizes the connection among people, animals and the environment. "While not every wild mammal is monitored for rabies, DEEP does include rabies testing for animals submitted to the Connecticut Veterinary Medical Diagnostic Laboratory for necropsy," the agency said. "In cases with human exposure, testing is closely coordinated with DPH and local health districts." The agency also cautioned against reading year-to-year increases as unusual on their own. "Rabies is a cyclical virus," DEEP said. "There will be years with low viral activity and as populations increase, exposure increases, and rates go up. As infected animals succumb to the virus, populations drop, and rabies rates decline. It is not unusual to have years with higher rates of infection." Unlike some states, Connecticut does not distribute rabies vaccine baits by aircraft, DEEP said. Massachusetts' long-running distribution of edible vaccine packets by helicopter recently got some attention amid the CDC warning. Aerial oral rabies vaccination programs are typically targeted efforts used where geography can help wildlife officials contain the disease. On Cape Cod , for example, officials have used vaccine baits as part of a long-running effort to reduce raccoon rabies, with the Cape Cod Canal serving as a partial physical barrier to animal movement. Oral vaccine baiting also is not a guarantee. Animals have to eat the bait, the effort must continue over time, and infected animals can still move into an area. The CDC advisory said national demand for rabies treatment has increased this year. The agency cited pharmacy utilization data showing rabies vaccine use up an estimated 33% and rabies immune globulin use up 76% as of Sept. 2, compared with the same period last year. The CDC said there is no national shortage, but it warned providers to administer treatment correctly. For people who have not previously been vaccinated against rabies, post-exposure treatment generally includes wound care, rabies immune globulin and a series of rabies vaccine doses. The CDC said errors can include administering vaccine in the wrong part of the body, failing to properly infiltrate immune globulin around the wound, giving immune globulin and vaccine in the same place, or unnecessarily restarting a vaccine series. The CDC said a typical rabies post-exposure prophylaxis course costs $11,000 to $14,000 per person. Rabies in the United States is now overwhelmingly associated with wildlife, not domestic dogs. Bats, raccoons, skunks and foxes are among the primary wildlife species that can carry rabies, though health officials emphasize that most wild animals are not rabid and that bats in particular play an important ecological role. The concern is direct contact, especially a bite, scratch or possible saliva exposure. DPH says residents should avoid contact with wild animals, keep pets vaccinated and contact local health officials after a possible exposure. DEEP said vaccination remains the most important step residents can take to reduce risk. "It is important for residents to remember that any mammal can carry the rabies virus and best way to reduce risk is to vaccinate your pets," the agency said. records.content: Sports Business News Life Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals CALIFORNIA California rabies incidents renew focus on a rare deadly virus Roseann Cattani USA TODAY NETWORK Updated Sept. 11, 2026, 1:52 p.m. PT California reported two rabies incidents involving humans this month, and a third animal tested positive earlier in May. But just how common is the virus that, once symptoms appear, is almost always fatal? While rabies in humans is very rare in the United States, public health officials advise residents and visitors, especially those with young children to be on the lookout for infected wildlife when out in nature. Earlier this month, public health officials in Humboldt County reminded residents not to handle bats after three children were treated for rabies exposure in two separate incidents, one in Manila, the other in Arcata. Bats from both of the incidents tested positive for the rabies virus. Exposure to infected bats can be especially tricky to notice, public health officials warn, with children most at risk. When Yosemite National Park announced last week that a bat they caught in May tested positive for rabies, they warned that "bat bites and scratches can be very small and may not always be visible or painful." Direct contact can also entail a bat touching the top of one's clothing or a wing brushing the skin or hair. The National Park Service (NPS) advised that "any direct contact with a bat, alive or dead, should be discussed with a healthcare provider." While no human contact with the "dead big brown bat found outside the Curry Village Showerhouse on May 18," was reported, according to the NPS, anyone who believes they may have done so should seek attention from a healthcare provider and contact the California Department of Health, which is working with the National Park Service on the case. The last rabies-positive bat discovered at Yosemite was in July 2025. Rabies exposure often comes from wildlife, bats Before the 1960s, dogs were a "common reservoir" of rabies in the United States, according to a CDC report analyzing human rabies deaths and exposure between 1938 and 2018. However, due to the widescale adoption of canine vaccination and leash laws starting in 1947, rabies control improved nationwide, the CDC found, so that by the late 1960s, fewer than 500 rabid dogs and three human rabies cases were reported annually. Now when rabies cases involving humans occur, they are generally due to exposure from infected wildlife. Animals most likely to transmit rabies, include bats, coyotes, foxes, raccoons and skunks, and in the United States, bats are the most likely culprit. Among the 89 cases of humans acquiring rabies in the United States between 1938 and 2018, per the CDC report, 70% were caused by infected bats. According to the National Park Service, less than 1% of bats in nature have rabies, "but bats that act strangely or contact humans are up to 10 times more likely to have rabies." How to spot and prevent rabies exposure Before heading out into nature, we understand we have to run through a mental checklist that includes mosquito repellent, sunscreen, and extra water. To protect ourselves and others from possible rabies exposure, public health officials advise the following. Fully vaccinate all domestic animals against rabies, including dogs (which is a state law), cats and select livestock. Avoid contact with wild and stray animals. Alive or dead. Bring pet food indoors at night. Report animal bites to a county or municipal animal control officer. If bitten, wash the bite immediately with soap and water and seek medical attention. When camping, ensure housing and overnight dwellings (tents or cabins) are sealed off from the outdoors. Make sure there are no small openings through which bats or other wildlife can enter. If this is not possible, sleeping under mosquito nets may prevent bats from contacting sleeping persons. Educate children to keep away from wildlife and stray animals. Any direct contact with a bat, alive or dead, should be discussed with a healthcare provider What happens if you're exposed to rabies? Treatment can prevent infection Rabies is one of the deadliest viruses known, but it is also one of the most preventable after an exposure. Here's what to know: Seek medical care immediately after any potential rabies exposure, including bites, scratches or direct contact with a bat. Wash wounds right away with soap and water. Treatment, called post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), typically includes: Rabies immune globulin (for unvaccinated people) A series of rabies vaccine shots over several weeks PEP is highly effective when given promptly after exposure. Once rabies symptoms appear, the disease is almost always fatal. Early symptoms can resemble the flu, then progress to confusion, hallucinations and difficulty swallowing. Because bat bites and scratches can be tiny and hard to detect, health officials recommend consulting a healthcare provider after any direct contact with a bat, even if no bite is visible. records.content: News Sports Business Opinion Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals CALIFORNIA California rabies incidents renew focus on a rare deadly virus Roseann Cattani USA TODAY NETWORK Updated Sept. 11, 2026, 4:52 p.m. ET California reported two rabies incidents involving humans this month, and a third animal tested positive earlier in May. But just how common is the virus that, once symptoms appear, is almost always fatal? While rabies in humans is very rare in the United States, public health officials advise residents and visitors, especially those with young children to be on the lookout for infected wildlife when out in nature. Earlier this month, public health officials in Humboldt County reminded residents not to handle bats after three children were treated for rabies exposure in two separate incidents, one in Manila, the other in Arcata. Bats from both of the incidents tested positive for the rabies virus. Exposure to infected bats can be especially tricky to notice, public health officials warn, with children most at risk. When Yosemite National Park announced last week that a bat they caught in May tested positive for rabies, they warned that "bat bites and scratches can be very small and may not always be visible or painful." Direct contact can also entail a bat touching the top of one's clothing or a wing brushing the skin or hair. The National Park Service (NPS) advised that "any direct contact with a bat, alive or dead, should be discussed with a healthcare provider." While no human contact with the "dead big brown bat found outside the Curry Village Showerhouse on May 18," was reported, according to the NPS, anyone who believes they may have done so should seek attention from a healthcare provider and contact the California Department of Health, which is working with the National Park Service on the case. The last rabies-positive bat discovered at Yosemite was in July 2025. Rabies exposure often comes from wildlife, bats Before the 1960s, dogs were a "common reservoir" of rabies in the United States, according to a CDC report analyzing human rabies deaths and exposure between 1938 and 2018. However, due to the widescale adoption of canine vaccination and leash laws starting in 1947, rabies control improved nationwide, the CDC found, so that by the late 1960s, fewer than 500 rabid dogs and three human rabies cases were reported annually. Now when rabies cases involving humans occur, they are generally due to exposure from infected wildlife. Animals most likely to transmit rabies, include bats, coyotes, foxes, raccoons and skunks, and in the United States, bats are the most likely culprit. Among the 89 cases of humans acquiring rabies in the United States between 1938 and 2018, per the CDC report, 70% were caused by infected bats. According to the National Park Service, less than 1% of bats in nature have rabies, "but bats that act strangely or contact humans are up to 10 times more likely to have rabies." How to spot and prevent rabies exposure Before heading out into nature, we understand we have to run through a mental checklist that includes mosquito repellent, sunscreen, and extra water. To protect ourselves and others from possible rabies exposure, public health officials advise the following. Fully vaccinate all domestic animals against rabies, including dogs (which is a state law), cats and select livestock. Avoid contact with wild and stray animals. Alive or dead. Bring pet food indoors at night. Report animal bites to a county or municipal animal control officer. If bitten, wash the bite immediately with soap and water and seek medical attention. When camping, ensure housing and overnight dwellings (tents or cabins) are sealed off from the outdoors. Make sure there are no small openings through which bats or other wildlife can enter. If this is not possible, sleeping under mosquito nets may prevent bats from contacting sleeping persons. Educate children to keep away from wildlife and stray animals. Any direct contact with a bat, alive or dead, should be discussed with a healthcare provider What happens if you're exposed to rabies? Treatment can prevent infection Rabies is one of the deadliest viruses known, but it is also one of the most preventable after an exposure. Here's what to know: Seek medical care immediately after any potential rabies exposure, including bites, scratches or direct contact with a bat. Wash wounds right away with soap and water. Treatment, called post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), typically includes: Rabies immune globulin (for unvaccinated people) A series of rabies vaccine shots over several weeks PEP is highly effective when given promptly after exposure. Once rabies symptoms appear, the disease is almost always fatal. Early symptoms can resemble the flu, then progress to confusion, hallucinations and difficulty swallowing. Because bat bites and scratches can be tiny and hard to detect, health officials recommend consulting a healthcare provider after any direct contact with a bat, even if no bite is visible. records.content: News Space Sports Restaurants Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals NEWS Rabies exposures rising nationwide. Is Florida at risk? Samantha Neely USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Sept. 11, 2026, 10:06 a.m. ET The CDC reported a 17% increase in rabies-related inquiries this summer compared to last year. Several recent rabies outbreaks have been reported, including one at a North Carolina petting zoo. Rabies is nearly 100% fatal but is preventable with appropriate post-exposure treatment. Inquiries for rabies-related cases spiked this summer, according to a new health advisory from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The CDC released a report on Thursday detailing a 17% increase in rabies-related inquiries compared with the same period in 2025, following several "high-profile rabies outbreaks and mass rabies exposure events." Just two weeks ago, a North Carolina petting zoo confirmed that several of its baby goats tested positive for rabies after being bit by a skunk and nearly 300 people were exposed. The report said at least eight United States jurisdictions reported increased use of rabies shots, errors in administering the post-exposure regimen, or both. Rabies is a zoonotic viral disease that primarily affects the central nervous system. An infected animal can spread rabies to humans and other animals through bites, scratches, or oral secretions, according to the CDC. The United States has around 4,000 to 5,000 confirmed animal rabies cases and fewer than 10 human rabies deaths each year. While the report did not highlight a specific animal these increases were tied to, the CDC did note reported increases in human rabies exposures involving known rabies vectors or animals in which rabies is less commonly reported. Are any of these increased cases in Florida? The CDC's report didn't highlight exactly where these increased cases came from. The USA TODAY NETWORK Florida reached out to the Florida Department of Health about current cases in the state and did not hear back at the time of publishing. However, Brevard County recently issued a rabies alert on Sept. 2 after a confirmed case of rabies in a raccoon captured in the Melbourne area off Andrews Avenue in Brevard County on Aug. 27. DOH-Brevard said it is monitoring rabies among wild animals in the area. Just days prior, St. Johns County also issued a rabies alert on Aug. 31 after a single confirmed case of rabies in a raccoon that was killed in the St. Augustine South area on Aug. 28. In 2025, the FDOH reported 117 total rabies cases, with most reported in Brevard. What animals are typically infected with rabies? According to the FDOH, the main wildlife sources of rabies in Florida are raccoons and bats. However, foxes, skunks, coyotes and even stray cats and dogs can carry rabies. Animals with rabies may exhibit strange behavior, such as being aggressive, attacking for no apparent reason, or acting very tame (for wild animals). They may not be able to eat, drink, or swallow, and may drool because they can't swallow their saliva. They will eventually die from the disease. The CDC warned the public to keep a distance from wildlife and to never approach animals that appear sick or injured. How deadly is rabies? The CDC says rabies is nearly 100% fatal, but it is preventable when post-exposure prophylaxis is given appropriately before the patient's symptoms start. Two rabies vaccines and two HRIG products are licensed for use in people in the United States. The report says clinicians should administer PEP appropriately because errors in rabies risk assessment and PEP administration could lead to unnecessary treatment, potential adverse effects, and avoidable costs. What do I do if I was bitten or exposed to rabies? The FDOH says that if you believe you may have been exposed to rabies, contact your health care provider and your county health department right away. The CDC says that if you or your pets have been in contact with any wildlife or sick-acting animals, particularly if you've been bitten or scratched, do the following: Wash any wounds immediately with water and soap (or water alone) for 15 minutes. Talk with a clinician or public health professional about your risk and if you might need rabies-related care. Tell your doctor about the type of animal you encountered and if you noted any signs that the animal was not acting normally. If the animal that bit you was not your pet, ask the owner for proof that the animal is up to date on their rabies vaccination. If you can do so safely, capture or confine the animal and contact your area’s animal control service or your health department for assistance. In some circumstances and in consultation with a veterinarian, observing an available animal might be a reasonable alternative to rabies testing. Samantha Neely is a trending reporter for the USA TODAY NETWORK-Florida, covering pop culture, theme parks, breaking news and more. records.content: Home News Health Politics Business Science Arts Travel Health Insurance Events Fashion Restaurants Saturday 12th September, 2026 Bat Rabies Detected in German County, Risk to Humans Low Wed 9th Sep, 2026 A bat found in Landkreis Bergstraße, Germany, has been confirmed to have bat rabies, according to local authorities. The bat, which exhibited unusually aggressive behavior, was taken to a rescue center where laboratory tests validated the suspicion of lyssavirus infection. Despite this discovery, local officials have assured residents that there is no immediate cause for alarm. While rabies in bats can, in theory, be transmitted to humans, the risk remains low. Human infection would require direct contact with an infected bat, such as through bites or scratches. Typically, bats are shy creatures that tend to avoid humans. Bats in Germany and other parts of Europe can harbor various lyssaviruses, which are related to the rabies virus. Nevertheless, these infections are distinct from the terrestrial rabies virus, considered eradicated in Germany since 2008. However, the presence of lyssavirus in bats does periodically surface. For instance, a case was recently confirmed in Rhineland-Palatinate in August, the first such detection since 2010. Rabies in bats, scientifically known as European Bat Lyssavirus (EBLV), is known to be present in several bat species across Europe. The virus can affect various types of bats, though actual transmission incidents to humans are rare. Transmission typically occurs only during interactions where a person is inadvertently exposed to the virus through close contact with an infected bat. The public is advised to exercise caution and avoid handling bats directly. Any bats found behaving abnormally should be reported to wildlife authorities or animal rescue centers for safe handling and testing. Bat conservation groups emphasize the importance of monitoring bat populations while ensuring public safety, given their ecological role and the relatively low risk to humans. Health authorities remind citizens that while the risk of rabies from bats remains low, actions should be taken to prevent contact, particularly in cases of finding a bat behaving erratically. Bats exhibiting signs of disorientation, aggression, or those found during the day in unusual locations should not be handled. With the recent detection of lyssavirus in bats in other regions, authorities across Germany maintain robust surveillance systems to monitor the health of wildlife populations. Such measures are in place to track the spread of any zoonotic diseases, ensuring early detection and intervention. The detection in Bergstraße serves as a reminder of the importance of continued vigilance in monitoring wildlife diseases that could pose a threat to public health. Scientists from several institutes remain actively involved in researching lyssaviruses to understand their transmission dynamics better and to evaluate the risk posed to humans and other animals. Public health campaigns stress the significance of rabies vaccinations for pets, as a preventive measure for any inadvertent interactions with wild animals. Although the likelihood of exposure via domestic animals is low, responsible pet ownership includes ensuring vaccinations are up to date. In cases of potential exposure, such as suffering a bat-bite, individuals are urged to seek immediate medical attention. Post-exposure prophylaxis is effective in preventing the onset of the disease if administered promptly. Bats play a crucial role in ecosystems, contributing to pest control and plant pollination. Conservationists argue that despite the potential health risks, bats should be protected and respected for their ecological contributions. They've urged the public to use protective measures like nets or bat boxes to safely direct them away from residential areas while preserving their habitats. As the lyssavirus case is managed in Bergstraße, authorities continue to work on educating the public about co-existing with wildlife, underscoring the crucial balance between conservation and public health safety. Efforts are ongoing to increase public awareness regarding the identification of rabies symptoms in wildlife and the necessary precautions to prevent the spread to humans. In a new health advisory , the CDC urged doctors to be on the lookout for possible exposures and to administer vaccines and treatments as needed. The agency also warned the public to avoid contact with wildlife and sick mammals, and to seek medical care if someone is bitten or scratched. The CDC sent the advisory through its Health Alert Network, the primary communication channel the agency uses to disseminate urgent public health information to doctors, hospital networks and health officials. Rabies is a rare but potentially fatal viral disease that must be treated before symptoms start. It spreads primarily through bites or scratches from an infected animal. Wildlife such as raccoons, skunks, bats and foxes are the most common carriers in the U.S. The CDC’s warning comes less than two weeks after North Carolina officials announced that three baby goats at a mobile petting zoo had tested positive for rabies , potentially exposing hundreds of people. The state health department launched a search to track down anyone who came into contact with the goats, saying Tuesday that rabies shots had been recommended for more than 260 people. The petting zoo, Farm Adventures, said the goats were too young for vaccination and had been bitten by a skunk found in their pen. Four goats were euthanized to prevent further spread, it said. In North Carolina, Franklin County Animal Control sets a trap in an area where a rabid skunk was found last summer. Marina Kopf / NBC News “Several high-profile rabies outbreaks and mass rabies exposure events have highlighted the importance of performing careful rabies risk assessments and following evidence-based recommendations for administering PEP [post-exposure prophylaxis],” the agency said. That post-exposure treatment typically includes a dose of an antibody medication that prevents infection, called human rabies immune globulin, and at least four doses of a rabies vaccine. The regimen is nearly 100% effective if administered quickly after exposure, according to the CDC. From July through August, the CDC said, it received 17% more rabies-related inquiries than during the same period last year and also received reports from at least eight state health departments about the increased use of rabies shots, or of errors in the administration of the post-exposure regimen. Not getting the shots before symptoms begin — typically, within weeks to months of an exposure — can lead to severe brain disease and death. More than 6 million people in the U.S. report animal bites each year, and around 100,000 are treated for rabies exposure. But fewer than 10 people in the U.S. die from rabies annually. A combination of pet vaccinations, animal control programs and human testing and treatment has significantly reduced the risk. Rabies exposures typically peak in the summer, since people tend to spend more time outdoors, which increases their odds of encountering wildlife. Hawaii is the only state in the U.S. that is free of rabies. In its health alert, the CDC warned the public to keep a distance from wildlife and to never approach animals that appear sick or injured. In such cases, contact local animal control, the agency said. “If you have pets, keep them up to date on rabies vaccines and away from wildlife when possible,” the CDC said in the alert. The agency also advises people to wash any bites or scratches right away with soap and water. Rebecca Lanning, whose family visited a dinosaur exhibit in Mocksville, North Carolina, on Aug. 15, previously told NBC News that she had been shocked to learn that her 4-year-old had been exposed to rabies. The exhibit included the mobile petting zoo with the goats that later tested positive. She rushed her son to the doctor for his first shots of the vaccine series. “My fear is that if he was feeding the goats, and he’s 4. Who’s to say that he didn’t touch his mouth or eyes?” Lanning said. “I don’t want to bury my child.”

Since July, multiple U.S. jurisdictions have reported local increases in human rabies exposures involving known rabies vectors or animals in which rabies is less commonly reported, according to the CDC. Several rabies outbreaks and mass exposure events have also been reported. From July through August, the CDC received 17% more rabies-related inquiries than during the same period in 2025, including reports involving multiple people. At least eight state health departments also reported increased use of rabies post-exposure prophylaxis, known as PEP, administration errors or both. Weekly pharmacy data as of Sept. 2 showed use of the two rabies vaccines licensed in the United States increased by an estimated 33% compared with the same period last year. Use of the two licensed rabies immunoglobulin products increased by an estimated 76%. The CDC said there is currently no shortage of human rabies vaccine or human rabies immunoglobulin in the United States. Rabies is a viral disease that is nearly 100% fatal but can be prevented when PEP is properly administered before symptoms begin, according to the CDC. Rabies can spread to humans and other animals through bites, scratches or oral secretions from an infected animal. The CDC said an estimated 1.4 million people in the United States seek medical care each year following animal contact and undergo an evaluation, while approximately 100,000 receive rabies PEP following a potential exposure. The agency is urging health departments and clinicians to conduct appropriate risk assessments before administering treatment and to follow recommendations for administering rabies vaccine and human rabies immune globulin. According to the CDC, a typical course of PEP can cost between $11,000 and $14,000 per person. Errors in assessing rabies risk or administering PEP can result in unnecessary treatment, potential adverse effects and avoidable costs. The CDC issued several recommendations for the public, including: Keep a safe distance from wildlife and do not approach animals that appear injured, sick or dead. Keep pets up to date on rabies vaccinations and away from wildlife when possible. After contact with wildlife or a sick-acting animal, particularly following a bite or scratch, immediately wash wounds with soap and water, or water alone, for 15 minutes. Contact a clinician or public health professional to discuss the exposure and whether rabies-related care may be necessary. Tell a doctor what type of animal was involved and whether it appeared to be behaving abnormally. If bitten by an animal that is not your pet, ask the owner for proof of current rabies vaccination. If it can be done safely, capture or confine the animal and contact local animal control or the health department for assistance. In some circumstances, and in consultation with a veterinarian, observing an available animal may be an alternative to rabies testing, according to the CDC. records.content: News Sports Tulare Entertainment Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals CALIFORNIA California rabies incidents renew focus on a rare deadly virus Roseann Cattani USA TODAY NETWORK Updated Sept. 11, 2026, 1:52 p.m. PT California reported two rabies incidents involving humans this month, and a third animal tested positive earlier in May. But just how common is the virus that, once symptoms appear, is almost always fatal? While rabies in humans is very rare in the United States, public health officials advise residents and visitors, especially those with young children to be on the lookout for infected wildlife when out in nature. Earlier this month, public health officials in Humboldt County reminded residents not to handle bats after three children were treated for rabies exposure in two separate incidents, one in Manila, the other in Arcata. Bats from both of the incidents tested positive for the rabies virus. Exposure to infected bats can be especially tricky to notice, public health officials warn, with children most at risk. When Yosemite National Park announced last week that a bat they caught in May tested positive for rabies, they warned that "bat bites and scratches can be very small and may not always be visible or painful." Direct contact can also entail a bat touching the top of one's clothing or a wing brushing the skin or hair. The National Park Service (NPS) advised that "any direct contact with a bat, alive or dead, should be discussed with a healthcare provider." While no human contact with the "dead big brown bat found outside the Curry Village Showerhouse on May 18," was reported, according to the NPS, anyone who believes they may have done so should seek attention from a healthcare provider and contact the California Department of Health, which is working with the National Park Service on the case. The last rabies-positive bat discovered at Yosemite was in July 2025. Rabies exposure often comes from wildlife, bats Before the 1960s, dogs were a "common reservoir" of rabies in the United States, according to a CDC report analyzing human rabies deaths and exposure between 1938 and 2018. However, due to the widescale adoption of canine vaccination and leash laws starting in 1947, rabies control improved nationwide, the CDC found, so that by the late 1960s, fewer than 500 rabid dogs and three human rabies cases were reported annually. Now when rabies cases involving humans occur, they are generally due to exposure from infected wildlife. Animals most likely to transmit rabies, include bats, coyotes, foxes, raccoons and skunks, and in the United States, bats are the most likely culprit. Among the 89 cases of humans acquiring rabies in the United States between 1938 and 2018, per the CDC report, 70% were caused by infected bats. According to the National Park Service, less than 1% of bats in nature have rabies, "but bats that act strangely or contact humans are up to 10 times more likely to have rabies." How to spot and prevent rabies exposure Before heading out into nature, we understand we have to run through a mental checklist that includes mosquito repellent, sunscreen, and extra water. To protect ourselves and others from possible rabies exposure, public health officials advise the following. Fully vaccinate all domestic animals against rabies, including dogs (which is a state law), cats and select livestock. Avoid contact with wild and stray animals. Alive or dead. Bring pet food indoors at night. Report animal bites to a county or municipal animal control officer. If bitten, wash the bite immediately with soap and water and seek medical attention. When camping, ensure housing and overnight dwellings (tents or cabins) are sealed off from the outdoors. Make sure there are no small openings through which bats or other wildlife can enter. If this is not possible, sleeping under mosquito nets may prevent bats from contacting sleeping persons. Educate children to keep away from wildlife and stray animals. Any direct contact with a bat, alive or dead, should be discussed with a healthcare provider What happens if you're exposed to rabies? Treatment can prevent infection Rabies is one of the deadliest viruses known, but it is also one of the most preventable after an exposure. Here's what to know: Seek medical care immediately after any potential rabies exposure, including bites, scratches or direct contact with a bat. Wash wounds right away with soap and water. Treatment, called post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), typically includes: Rabies immune globulin (for unvaccinated people) A series of rabies vaccine shots over several weeks PEP is highly effective when given promptly after exposure. Once rabies symptoms appear, the disease is almost always fatal. Early symptoms can resemble the flu, then progress to confusion, hallucinations and difficulty swallowing. Because bat bites and scratches can be tiny and hard to detect, health officials recommend consulting a healthcare provider after any direct contact with a bat, even if no bite is visible. In a video recently posted to Instagram, Daniel Carrai (@danielcarrai) said he recently directed the production for the band SLIDE, incorporating several baby goats into the scenes. Cast and crew members held and interacted with the animals, unaware of any danger until weeks later, when production members learned the goats were infected. The animals originated from Farm Adventures, based in Harmony, North Carolina, that transported livestock to events across the state during the summer. According to the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services (NCDHHS), officials believe a skunk entered the animals' pen in late July. In a post on Facebook late last month, Farm Adventures explained that “the baby goats were kept in a separate pen, away from the others, and were too young to receive their vaccinations.” The company added that it “unfortunately encountered a skunk in their pen, which we promptly removed and disposed of. However, during this process, the skunk was able to bite the goats.” The farm said it had "no clue the goats had gotten bit" since they showed no signs of rabies. “Trust me if we did we would not [have] spent $100s of dollars for vets,” they added. “We will be closely monitoring our remaining animals under the guidelines provided by health officials,” the farm wrote. By August 29, three of the goats tested positive and were euthanized alongside a fourth presumed case that went untested. State health alerts indicated the animals could have been infectious between July 28 and August 27, having made appearances in at least seven counties. Public appearances included an assisted living facility in Statesville on July 28, a back-to-school event in Lexington on August 1, another assisted living facility in Statesville on August 6 and the Masonic Picnic Grounds in Mocksville on August 15. The goats also attended private events in Mecklenburg, Watauga, Burke, Durham and Iredell counties, the NCDHHS said. “Anyone who had contact with baby goats” from the petting zoo during the exposure window should contact a local health department, officials added. Although transmission from livestock is considered a lower risk than a bite from a wild animal, infected saliva can spread the virus through broken skin or the eyes, nose or mouth. Carrai stated in his Instagram video that approximately 20 people involved with the video production faced potential exposure, prompting immediate medical concerns. In a comment on the post, Carrai explained that one concern was the possibility that someone could have touched their face after coming into contact with the goats' saliva. Newsweek reached out to Carrai via email for additional information and comment. What Are the Symptoms of Rabies? Rabies remains a fatal virus that attacks the central nervous system, though human cases are exceedingly rare in the United States. North Carolina has not recorded a human case since 2011, according to the NCDHHS. Nationwide, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports that about 1.4 million Americans seek medical evaluation for potential exposure annually, with fewer than 10 deaths recorded each year due to robust prevention protocols. Wild animals—primarily raccoons, skunks, and foxes—pose a threat to three-quarters of the U.S. population. The virus spreads through infected saliva, typically via bites or scratches. While symptoms can take weeks or months to appear, early signs mimic the flu, such as weakness, fever or headache, and are often accompanied by irritation at the wound site. As the disease progresses, it takes one of two forms: While extremely dangerous and potentially fatal, rabies is preventable but requires vaccination or immediate medical attention after exposure, according to the CDC. Post-exposure prophylaxis, which includes wound washing, human rabies immune globulin, and rabies vaccine, is highly effective if received soon after exposure. Because baby goats are often bottle-fed, cuddled, and handled closely, including and especially in petting zoos, the likelihood of direct contact with an infected animal is high. The Financial Impact of Prevention For those affected, the incident brought significant financial strain alongside health worries. Carrai noted in his video that medical treatment for himself and his wife could approach $20,000, as their health insurance did not cover the necessary treatment. Rabies Warning Issued in Multiple States Health officials in several states have issued rabies warnings after infected bats, raccoons, foxes, goats and a pet dog were detected this year, raising concerns about possible exposure among people and pets. The alerts include sharp local increases in Idaho and Texas. Idaho has detected 24 rabid bats so far this year—more than in any of the previous three years—while one public health district has received more than twice as many calls about possible bat exposures as it had at the same point last year. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has issued a health alert saying that, since July, there has been an increase in human exposure to rabies, including in areas were rabies cases are not common. If you were bitten or scratched by a mammal, you should wash the wound with water and soap for several minutes get preventive care right away, and, if available use a virucidal agent such as a povidone-iodine solution. You should also see a healthcare provider if you came into contact with a bat, even if there is no apparent wound on your body. The CDC advises that bat scratches and bites can be so small that they go unnoticed by humans. In the U.S., rabies cases are more common in the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast states according to the CDC. What is rabies? Is rabies fatal? Rabies is viral disease caused by multiple viruses of the Lyssavirus genus. The CDC describes the disease as a fatal, acute and progressive infection that attacks the central nervous system. The disease fatality rate is near 100%, but the disease is preventable if post-exposure medicine is taken soon after the exposure and before symptoms appear. The most common form of transmission is through the bite of a rabid animal. Scratches can also spread the disease, according to the CDC. What animals are likely to carry rabies? All mammals can contract rabies and are believed to be able to carry it as well. Now some mammals are much more likely to be rabid and transmit it to other mammals. Mammals that commonly carry rabies are bats, racoons, skunks and foxes. According to the CDC these animals are responsible for 90% of reported cases. Dogs and cats can also infect humans with rabies, especially stray, unvaccinated dogs and cats. According to CDC data collected between 2019 and 2023, these are the most common animal rabies across the U.S.: East Coast states- Racoons and bats. Texas- Skunks and bats. Arizona and Southern California- Skunks, bats and gray foxes. Colorado- Skunks and bats. Illinois- Bats. Dakotas- Skunks and bats. By Asher Klein • Published September 12, 2026 • Updated on September 12, 2026 at 1:41 am Log in or create a free profile to save articles BOOKMARKER Getty Images A bat showed signs of having rabies at a Providence, Rhode Island, zoo last month, health officials said Friday. Visitors spotted the bat by the Roger Williams Park Zoo water play area on Aug. 24, the Rhode Island Department of Health said, noting that they'd been informed on Friday, leading to an investigation. Stream NBC10 Boston news for free, 24/7, wherever you are. WATCH HERE Health official said that a zoo veterinarian had told them there was low risk that humans had been exposed and that the bat was discarded safely, following the zoo's protocol. While it couldn't be tested for rabies, health officials shared the news Friday so that anyone who came into contact with the bat before Aug. 24 can reach out to epidemiologists so they can be evaluated, in case they need treatment. The agency's Center for Acute Infectious Disease Epidemiology is available Monday-Friday 8:30 a.m.-4:30 p.m. at 401-222-2577 and at other times at 401-276-8046. NBC10 Boston has reached out to the zoo for any response to what happened. 2:29 Child and woman bitten in separate fox attacks hours apart in Worcester neighborhood Zena Bottom was attacked by a fox Thursday morning after Janessa Williams was injured the evening before. Police said a fox has been euthanized and is being tested for rabies. Rabies can be fatal if it's not quickly treated, and on Thursday, health officials said, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention issued an advisory warning about an uptick in rabid animals and people being exposed. Rhode Island has seen more rabid animals -- mostly bats and raccoons -- this year as well.
